DynamAuction: A Reinforcement Learning Environment for Repeated Auctions with Dynamic Value

Eugénie Patard ††thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: INRIA, FairPlay Joint Team    Corentin Pla11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: INRIA, FairPlay Joint Team    Benjamin Heymann ††thanks: Equal supervision Affiliation: INRIA, FairPlay Joint Team    Patrick Loiseau22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: INRIA, FairPlay Joint Team Affiliation:  Criteo AI Lab Affiliation:  CREST-ENSAEParis, France
Abstract

A buyer who repeatedly participates in auctions for related items often faces a dynamic value problem: what they win today changes what tomorrow’s items are worth. Despite the empirical importance of such effects, especially in display advertising, the algorithmic literature on repeated auctions has largely focused on the learning problem, by treating each opportunity as a contextual bandit, while sidestepping the planning problem induced by the dependence of current value on past wins. We introduce DynamAuction, a synthetic environment for single-buyer sequential bidding. The reward from each win depends on the buyer’s history of previous wins, summarized through a carry-over state. The environment supports first- and second-price auctions, non-homogeneous Poisson arrivals, delayed feedback, saturation, and recency effects. We also introduce a new class of Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithms. On our benchmark scenario, these MPC policies outperform off-the-shelf deep RL baselines (PPO, SAC, TD3) as well as a tuned shading baseline. We release DynamAuction to support RL research on repeated auctions.

DynamAuction

1 Introduction

Motivation.

In many real-world bidding settings, a buyer participates in a long sequence of auctions for related items, and the marginal value of winning the next one depends on what they have already won. The simplest instance is a buyer with single-unit demand: a firm that needs to acquire exactly one piece of equipment over a quarter through a series of auctions derives no additional value from a second win, so the value of the next opportunity drops to zero as soon as one auction has been won. More complex dynamics arise in display advertising. For example, showing the same banner to a user multiple times within a short period typically leads to diminishing returns, so the value of the next impression depends on the timing and outcomes of previous auctions.

Learning vs. planning in repeated auctions.

Most existing work on repeated auctions focuses on learning how much to bid from contextual information and an unknown competition distribution Weed et al. (2016); Achddou et al. (2021); Flajolet and Jaillet (2017). The only planning component typically included is a global budget or ROI constraint, which couples bids over time through a Lagrangian or dual variable Flajolet and Jaillet (2017); Wang et al. (2023); Balseiro and Gur (2017); Balseiro et al. (2020). Beyond this constraint, these approaches generally assume that the value of each opportunity depends only on its current context, without accounting for how past wins affect future values. In many applications, improving planning by accounting for these dynamics may be more beneficial than further improving learning under a static value model. Our work aims to study this question by introducing a reinforcement learning environment in which these dependencies can be explicitly modeled and evaluated.

Motivations for a synthetic environment.

Evaluating bidding algorithms on real-world data presents several challenges. Logged auction data only reflect the decisions made by the bidding policy used to collect them, making it difficult to evaluate alternative strategies without additional assumptions. Online evaluation through A/B tests is the textbook alternative, but it is slow, costly, constrained by business and ethical risk, and does not let the researcher independently vary delay, saturation, recency, or interference. A simulator avoids these limitations by allowing each factor to be varied under controlled conditions. Although DynamAuction can be used with general reinforcement learning algorithms, our experiments focus on planning and on the value of accounting for past wins.

Contributions.

  • •

    We formalize a model of single-buyer sequential bidding in which the per-display reward is generated by a kernel conditioned on a carry-over context obtained by aggregating past wins through a commutative monoid. This framework accommodates delayed feedback, saturation and recency effects, exogenous interference, and user heterogeneity.

  • •

    We release DynamAuction, an open-source, Gymnasium-compatible implementation of this model, together with a default benchmark task and guidelines for users to define new tasks.

  • •

    We implement and evaluate a panel of baselines (constant bid, prediction-based bidding, greedy myopic bidding with shading, PPO, SAC, TD3) and introduce a class of Model Predictive Control algorithms. We show empirically that, on the benchmark scenario, this myopic-optimal MPC outperforms the deep-RL baselines and a tuned shading baseline.

Outline.

Section 2 reviews the related literature and motivates the design of the environment. Section 3 presents the model, and Section 4 introduces DynamAuction. Section 5 describes our MPC approach. Section 6 presents the experiments, and Section 7 concludes. We use display advertising as the main running example throughout the paper. Accordingly, we refer to a won auction as a display and sometimes to its reward as a conversion.

2 Related work

2.1 Repeated auctions, attribution, and budget/ROI constraints

Much of the literature on repeated auctions studies a single bidder facing an unknown competition distribution, using bandit Lattimore and Szepesvári (2020) or online learning methods. For example, Weed et al. (2016); Achddou et al. (2021) consider repeated second-price auctions where the bidder learns the value of an item only after winning it. They develop bidding strategies with theoretical guarantees in stochastic and adversarial settings. Other works extend this framework to include global budget or ROI constraints, often using knapsack formulations Balseiro and Gur (2017); Balseiro et al. (2020); Castiglioni et al. (2022); Castiglioni et al. (2024); Flajolet and Jaillet (2017); Feng et al. (2023); Heymann (2019). This perspective has received considerable attention in the theoretical literature and has led to several important modeling contributions Balseiro et al. (2017); Balseiro et al. (2015); Conitzer et al. (2022). A recent survey is provided in Aggarwal et al. (2024).

A second line of work uses reinforcement learning (RL) to model sequential bidding as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Cai et al. (2017) formulate real-time bidding as an MDP whose state encodes the campaign’s remaining budget and lifetime together with the current bid request, and learn a value-function approximation for the resulting bidding policy. Wu et al. (2018) propose a model-free RL approach for budget-constrained bidding, while Yang et al. (2019) treat bid optimization as a multivariable control problem for a set of campaigns. A more general RL framework with budget and KPI constraints is introduced in He et al. (2021). More recent work has questioned whether the current state contains enough information for effective bidding decisions. This has motivated generative approaches that model entire bidding trajectories rather than relying only on the current state Guo et al. (2024); Peng et al. (2025). However, these approaches mainly capture dependencies between bidding decisions through campaign-level constraints, such as budgets or ROI targets. The value of an impression is generally determined by its current context, without explicitly modeling how previous wins affect the value of future opportunities.

A third line of work focuses on attributing observed conversions back to the displays that caused them, and on bidding directly on incremental rather than observed outcomes. The general framing of computational advertising as a counterfactual learning problem goes back to Bottou et al. (2013). On the bidding side, Diemert Eustache, Meynet Julien et al. (2017) show empirically that attribution-aware bidding outperforms last-touch baselines, and Bompaire et al. (2021) and Bompaire et al. (2024) develop causal models for repeated user interactions, the latter introducing the myopic-optimal valuation that we will reuse. Lewis and Wong (2022) formalize the link between incrementality and attribution. Heymann et al. (2024) introduce the concept of repeated auctions with dynamic value and consider a setting simple enough to be solved with a differential equation, Heymann and Sakhi (2026) leverage the analysis to build a no-regret learning algorithm based on plugin estimators, and Badanidiyuru Varadaraja et al. (2022) study incrementality bidding via reinforcement learning under mixed and delayed rewards. These works highlight the importance of accounting for past interactions, diminishing returns, and delayed outcomes. Our environment allows these effects to be modeled explicitly and studied under controlled conditions.

2.2 RL benchmarks, simulators, and datasets for auctions

A growing collection of open resources targets the bidding problem in online advertising. We list below those most relevant to our work.

Datasets. These contributions mostly cast the auction as a supervised learning problem. Liao et al. (2014); Zhang et al. (2014) release the iPinYou dataset, the first publicly available large-scale RTB log, consisting of ≈35\approx 35 GB of bid, impression, click, and conversion logs from a 2013 DSP competition. No environment for off-policy evaluation is provided. Diemert Eustache, Meynet Julien et al. (2017) release the Criteo Attribution Modeling for Bidding dataset, which contains 30 days of real advertising data with attribution labels. The dataset can be used to study attribution and incrementality, but does not provide an environment for simulating auction outcomes under different bidding strategies.

Simulators. Jeunen et al. (2023) release AuctionGym: a Python simulator of first- and second-price advertising auctions designed for the off-policy evaluation of bandit-style learning-to-bid algorithms. It provides configurable competition; however, the per-impression value is a function of the current context only.

Datasets paired with simulators. More recently, Su et al. (2024) release the simulated environment of the Alibaba/NeurIPS 2024 auto-bidding competition: it consists of a large dataset and an RL-ready state/action/reward interface designed for cost-per-action-constrained bidding. Khirianova et al. (2025) release BAT, a benchmark built on the Avito platform, comprising 10 million first-price and 1 million Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) auction records collected over a month, together with a simulator and budget-pacing and cost-per-click (CPC) constrained baselines.

None of these resources is designed to exhibit the dependence of a single bidder’s per-opportunity value on the history of past wins. DynamAuction is therefore complementary: AuctionGym, BAT, and the AuctionNet environment are natural sandboxes for studying learning-to-bid and budget/ROI/Cost Per Auction (CPA)-constrained pacing; the iPinYou and Criteo datasets are appropriate for Click-Through Rate (CTR)/Conversion Rate (CVR) and attribution modeling on real logs; and DynamAuction is intended as a sandbox for studying planning under the dynamics induced by past wins on the value of future opportunities.

2.3 Model Predictive Control and model-based RL

Model Predictive Control (MPC) Camacho and Bordons (2013) uses a predictive model to optimize a sequence of actions over a finite horizon, executes only the first action, and replans at the next decision step. By evaluating candidate actions through model predictions rather than direct interactions with the environment, MPC is particularly appealing in settings where real-world experimentation is costly, provided that a sufficiently accurate model is available. MPC is an instance of a broader class of model-based approaches that use learned or known dynamics to guide decision-making. In model-based reinforcement learning, these approaches are commonly distinguished by how and when the model is used. In decision-time planning, the model is used at each decision step to evaluate candidate action sequences and select an action. PETS (Chua et al., 2018) is a representative example, as are the MPC algorithms proposed in Section 5. In background planning, the model is used during training to simulate trajectories and improve a policy or value function. Unlike decision-time planning, these methods learn a policy using model-generated trajectories, rather than using the model to optimize actions at each decision step. MBPO (Janner et al., 2019) and Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020) follow this approach. MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020) combines elements of both: it learns a compact latent dynamics model used for decision-time planning through Monte Carlo tree search, while training the model to support value and reward predictions rather than reconstructing the full environment. Model-based approaches have also been explored in real-time bidding, primarily to address budget allocation, pacing, and ROI or CPA constraints (Cai et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2023). In contrast, our setting focuses on a different source of temporal dependence: rather than campaign-level constraints, past auction wins influence the future marginal value of targeting the same user. The closest related work is repeated bidding with dynamic valuations (Heymann et al., 2024). Building on this perspective, DynamAuction provides a configurable benchmark for studying such sequential bidding decisions.

2.4 Benchmark Design Requirements

Based on the literature reviewed above, we identify three key properties for benchmarking sequential bidding with dynamic valuations. Delayed feedback. The reward from winning an auction may be observed only after a stochastic delay, which can be long. Diminishing returns. The marginal value of winning an auction may decrease as the bidder accumulates wins for the same user, reflecting saturation effects. Recency effects. The marginal value of a win may also depend on the time elapsed since previous wins, rather than only on their number. Beyond these three properties, the environment should allow for heterogeneous users, exogenous events affecting user behavior, different opponent bid distributions and auction formats, and configurable auction arrival processes. We do not consider campaign-level budget or ROI constraints, which have been extensively studied and are separate from the user-level dynamics considered here. They could nevertheless be incorporated in future extensions.

3 Model: sequential bidding with carry-over value

3.1 Buyer, opportunities, and arrival process

We consider a single buyer interacting over a finite, possibly random, time horizon [0,T][0,T] where T>0T>0, with a user uu drawn from a set 𝒰\mathcal{U} according to a probability measure ρ\rho. 3.2 Carry-over context as a commutative monoid

To capture the dependence of the buyer’s per-opportunity value on past wins, we summarize the user’s display history into a single state. We fix a (measurable) space33 3 In what follows, we omit most of the measurability assumptions. 𝒮\mathcal{S} together with a commutative monoid44 4 A monoid is a set equipped with an associative binary operation and an identity element. structure (𝒮,⊕,𝟎)(\mathcal{S},\oplus,\mathbf{0}). The binary operation ⊕:𝒮×𝒮→𝒮\oplus:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} is associative and commutative, and 𝟎∈𝒮\mathbf{0}\in\mathcal{S} is its identity element. We further fix a decay map γ:𝒳×[0,T]×[0,T]→𝒮,(x,t′,t)↦γ⁡(x,t′,t)\gamma:\mathcal{X}\times[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathcal{S},\quad(x,t^{\prime},t)\mapsto\gamma(x,t^{\prime},t), intended to be evaluated only at t′≤tt^{\prime}\leq t, and which encodes the residual contribution at time tt of a display with feature xx that was shown at the earlier time t′t^{\prime}. For a fixed user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} with realized win sequence (ti,xi)i∈ℐu​(t)(t_{i},x_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{u}(t)} at time t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], we define the carry-over context at time tt as

Su​(t)=⨁i∈ℐu​(t)γ⁡(xi,ti,t)∈𝒮,\displaystyle S_{u}(t)\;=\;\bigoplus_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{u}(t)}\gamma(x_{i},t_{i},t)\;\in\;\mathcal{S}, (1)

with the empty sum convention Su​(t)=𝟎S_{u}(t)=\mathbf{0} when ℐu​(t)=∅\mathcal{I}_{u}(t)=\emptyset. Since ⊕\oplus is associative and commutative, the value of the sum does not depend on the order in which past wins are aggregated. By construction, SuS_{u} is càdlàg in tt: it jumps at each win time tit_{i} and evolves smoothly between wins, through the dependence of γ\gamma on its third argument. Familiar instances of (𝒮,⊕,𝟎)(\mathcal{S},\oplus,\mathbf{0}) that we use in the experiments include (ℝ≥0,+,0)(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},+,0) for additive counters, ([0,1],×,1)([0,1],\times,1) for multiplicatively decreasing marginal effects, and ([0,+∞],min,+∞)([0,+\infty],\min,+\infty) for the time since the most recent qualifying win. For the recency context, a qualifying display contributes γ⁡(x,t′,t)=t−t′\gamma(x,t^{\prime},t)=t-t^{\prime}, while a nonqualifying display contributes +∞+\infty. Taking the minimum gives the time since the most recent qualifying win, or +∞+\infty if there has been none. A different choice is to retain the full display history. We use (𝖧,∪,∅)(\mathsf{H},\cup,\emptyset), where 𝖧\mathsf{H} is the collection of finite sets of display–time pairs (xi,ti)(x_{i},t_{i}). Each display contributes γ⁡(x,t′,t)={(x,t′)}\gamma(x,t^{\prime},t)=\{(x,t^{\prime})\}, and these contributions are combined by set union. The timestamps allow us to recover the chronological order of the displays.

3.3 Reward kernel

We define a reward kernel that describes how the expected reward of a display is distributed over time. It is modeled as a positive measure over conversion delays, parametrized by the user, the displayed item, the carry-over context at the time of display, and an exogenous information process (introduced in Section 3.4). Formally, we define a measurable map

𝒦:𝒰×𝒳×𝒮×𝒴×[0,T]→ℳ+​([0,∞)),\mathcal{K}:\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{Y}\times[0,T]\;\to\;\mathcal{M}_{+}\bigl([0,\infty)\bigr),

where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the value space of the exogenous information process and ℳ+​([0,∞))\mathcal{M}_{+}\bigl([0,\infty)\bigr) denotes the set of positive Borel measures on [0,∞)[0,\infty). For a display occurring at time tt, the kernel specifies the expected reward associated with different delays after the display. For any Borel measurable set A⊆[0,∞)A\subseteq[0,\infty) of such delays, we write

𝒦⁡(u,x,s,y,t)​(A)=κ⁡(u,x,s,y,t)​δ0​(A)+∫Aλ⁡(u,x,s,y,t,τ)​𝑑τ,\mathcal{K}(u,x,s,y,t)(A)\;=\;\kappa(u,x,s,y,t)\delta_{0}(A)\;+\;\int_{A}\lambda(u,x,s,y,t;\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau, (2)

where the Dirac component κ\kappa models the instantaneous part of the reward, while the absolutely continuous component λ\lambda models the delayed part as a density over the delay τ≥0\tau\geq 0 since the display. For a single won display at time tit_{i} on user uu with feature xix_{i}, the expected reward attributable to this display and generated over a time window [ti,ti+h][t_{i},t_{i}+h] for h≥0h\geq 0 is

ri​(h)=κ⁡(u,xi,Su​(ti−),yu​(ti),ti)+∫0hλ⁡(u,xi,Su​(ti−),yu​(ti),ti,τ)​𝑑τ,r_{i}(h)\;=\;\kappa\bigl(u,x_{i},S_{u}(t_{i}^{-}),y_{u}(t_{i}),t_{i}\bigr)\;+\;\int_{0}^{h}\lambda\bigl(u,x_{i},S_{u}(t_{i}^{-}),y_{u}(t_{i}),t_{i};\,\tau\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\tau, (3)

where Su​(ti−)S_{u}(t_{i}^{-}) denotes the left-limit of the carry-over context at tit_{i}, i.e., the carry-over context evaluated just before the ii-th win is incorporated into it.55 5 The left-limit convention ensures that a winning bid is rewarded against the context that justified placing it, rather than against a context that already includes the consequence of the win itself. The buyer’s expected cumulative reward over the horizon [0,T][0,T] is then obtained by integrating per-display contributions over all wins occurring before TT against the population measure ρ\rho,

ℛ⁡(T)=∫𝒰𝔼⁡[∑i∈ℐu​(T)ri​(T−ti)]​ρ​(𝑑u),\mathcal{R}(T)\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{u}(T)}r_{i}(T-t_{i})\,\right]\rho(\mathrm{d}u), (4)

where the expectation is over the arrival process, the item-feature distribution, the competition, the exogenous process, and any randomness in the bidding policy, all conditional on the user uu. The expected cumulative payment is 𝒞(T)=∫𝒰𝔼[∑j:θj≤Tp(bj,Bj)]ρ(du),\mathcal{C}(T)\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\sum_{j:\theta_{j}\leq T}p(b_{j},B_{j})\,\right]\rho(\mathrm{d}u), and the buyer’s net cumulative profit ℛ⁡(T)−𝒞⁡(T)\mathcal{R}(T)-\mathcal{C}(T) is what they seek to maximize.

3.4 Exogenous information and information available to the buyer

Exogenous information process.

For each user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, we allow exogenous events that affect the value of future displays but are independent of the buyer’s actions. These events occur at times 0≤τ1u<τ2u<⋯0\leq\tau_{1}^{u}<\tau_{2}^{u}<\cdots and have marks eℓu∈ℰe_{\ell}^{u}\in\mathcal{E}. We treat the marked point process Πu=(eℓu,τℓu)ℓ≥1\Pi_{u}=(e_{\ell}^{u},\tau_{\ell}^{u})_{\ell\geq 1} as a primitive of the model and assume it is independent of the buyer’s bidding policy. We then summarize the past of this process into a càdlàg exogenous information process

yu:[0,T]→𝒴,yu​(t)=Ψ⁡({(eℓu,τℓu):τℓu≤t}),\displaystyle y_{u}:[0,T]\to\mathcal{Y},\qquad y_{u}(t)\;=\;\Psi\bigl(\{(e_{\ell}^{u},\tau_{\ell}^{u}):\tau_{\ell}^{u}\leq t\}\bigr), (5)

The resulting state yu​(t)y_{u}(t) affects the reward generated by a display at time tt but evolves independently of the buyer’s actions.

Information available to the buyer.

Let ϕ:𝒮×[0,∞)→𝒪S\phi:\mathcal{S}\times[0,\infty)\to\mathcal{O}_{S} be a measurable observation map, where 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S} is the space of reported carry-over summaries. Full observation corresponds to 𝒪S=𝒮\mathcal{O}_{S}=\mathcal{S} and ϕ⁡(s,t)=s\phi(s,t)=s. At an opportunity time θj\theta_{j} on user uu, we assume the buyer observes the candidate item feature xjx_{j}, the user identity uu, the carry-over summary ϕ⁡(Su​(θj−),θj)\phi(S_{u}(\theta_{j}^{-}),\theta_{j}), the exogenous process value yu​(θj)y_{u}(\theta_{j}), and the time θj\theta_{j} itself. We collect this information in the observable state.

Zj=(u,Xj,ϕ⁡(Su​(θj−),θj),yu​(θj),θj)∈𝒰×𝒳×𝒪S×𝒴×[0,∞).Z_{j}=\bigl(u,X_{j},\phi(S_{u}(\theta_{j}^{-}),\theta_{j}),y_{u}(\theta_{j}),\theta_{j}\bigr)\in\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}_{S}\times\mathcal{Y}\times[0,\infty).

After each auction, the buyer observes the win indicator and payment. The scenario specifies whether the competing bid BjB_{j} is also disclosed and how delayed rewards are reported. Policies may use current and past observations, past bids, feedback already received, and private randomization. The observation ZjZ_{j} need not be Markov. Writing bj=π⁡(Zj)b_{j}=\pi(Z_{j}) restricts attention to policies using only the current observation. Figure 1 summarizes the interaction process.

4 DynamAuction

DynamAuction implements the model introduced in the previous section as a Gymnasium environment. It allows researchers to evaluate bidding strategies under different auction dynamics through configurable parameters and provides a set of baseline policies for comparison. Additional information is provided in Appendix A.

Scenario configuration.

In DynamAuction, a scenario defines the model parameters, including auction mechanism, reward kernel, carry-over context, competition distribution, campaign horizon, and arrival process. Scenarios can be saved and reused across experiments, making it easy to compare bidding strategies under the same conditions. Table 2 presents the predefined scenarios available in DynamAuction.

Gymnasium interface.

DynamAuction follows the Gymnasium API (Towers et al., 2024) and can be used with RL libraries such as Stable-Baselines3 (Raffin et al., 2021). We provide three wrappers to adapt the environment for RL training (Table 3). The recommended order is: (i) oracle masking, which removes expected-reward information that would not be available to a real bidder; (ii) observation flattening, which converts the observations into a single vector for standard neural network policies; and (iii) bid clipping, which limits bids to [0,bmax][0,b_{\max}] during training for stable exploration.

5 Model Predictive Control with Myopic Valuations

5.1 Myopic-optimal valuation

The planning problem introduced in Section 3 can, in principle, be solved using dynamic programming. The optimal bid at time tt must account not only for the reward obtained by winning the current auction, but also for its impact on future rewards. As shown in (Bompaire et al., 2021, Theorem 3.1), this trade-off can be characterized using the Bellman value function V⋆V^{\star}, which represents the maximum expected cumulative reward achievable from a given state zz. However, estimating V⋆V^{\star} is challenging. The state space is high-dimensional, online exploration is costly, offline counterfactual estimation suffers from high variance, and the environment is non-stationary. Instead, we build on the notion of myopic-optimal valuation introduced in Bompaire et al. (2024). The myopic-optimal value V0V_{0} is defined as the optimal bid for the current display under two assumptions: (i) the bidder cannot participate in any future auction on the same user, and (ii) the current auction is second-price. In our model, V0V_{0} corresponds to the expected reward generated by the current display, obtained by integrating Equation (3) over the full delay support. It can be estimated using a fixed continuation policy that places no further bids on the same user, thereby isolating the reward of the current display from future bidding decisions. Additional algorithmic details are provided in Appendix B.

5.2 Planning with Myopic-optimal Valuations

At each decision step, our Model Predictive Control (MPC) approach compares candidate bids through Monte Carlo rollouts over a finite planning horizon. It submits the bid with the highest estimated net reward and replans at the next auction. An estimator V^0\widehat{V}_{0} of the myopic-optimal value provides the scale for both the candidate bids and a fixed continuation policy. Rollout scores are computed from simulated conversions and payments. Thus, the optimization concerns a single multiplier for the current bid, while accounting for its consequences for future opportunities.

Candidate bid. We express each candidate bid as a multiple of the estimated myopic-optimal value:

b⁡(α,Z)=α​V^0​(Z),b(\alpha;Z)=\alpha\widehat{V}_{0}(Z), (6)

where α∈𝒜0⊂ℝ≥0\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{0}\subset\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is selected from a finite set of candidate multipliers. In a second-price auction, α=1\alpha=1 bids the estimated myopic value, while α<1\alpha<1 allows the planner to reduce the bid when winning the current auction has an adverse effect on future opportunities.

Simulating future auctions. At auction ii, at time θi\theta_{i}, we generate MM rollouts from copies of the current simulator state, retaining past wins and pending conversions. The current observation ZiZ_{i} is held fixed, while the remaining campaign duration and future events are resampled according to the scenario model. Let LmL_{m} denote the last auction time in the complete sampled campaign, including the current auction. The planning window contains the auction indices 𝒩H(m)\mathcal{N}_{H}^{(m)} with θi≤θk(m)≤min⁡(θi+H,Lm)\theta_{i}\leq\theta_{k}^{(m)}\leq\min(\theta_{i}+H,L_{m}), where HH is measured in time units. The current auction uses b⁡(α,Zi)b(\alpha;Z_{i}), and all subsequent auctions in this window use b⁡(αcont,Zk(m))b(\alpha_{\mathrm{cont}};Z_{k}^{(m)}), with αcont\alpha_{\mathrm{cont}} fixed across candidates. The continuation rule is fixed, but its bids depend on the observations reached in each rollout. All candidates are evaluated on the same sampled campaigns, using common random numbers for competing bids, display features, and conversions, with draws aligned by auction to reduce the variance of score differences.

Evaluating simulated trajectories. For each simulated win, the display’s conversions are sampled using its pre-win carry-over context. Let Ck,Lm(m)C_{k,L_{m}}^{(m)} denote the total value of these conversions occurring no later than LmL_{m}. The contribution of auction kk to the rollout score is

gk(m)​(α)=𝒲⁡(bk(m),Bk(m))​Ck,Lm(m)−p⁡(bk(m),Bk(m)),g_{k}^{(m)}(\alpha)=\mathcal{W}\!\left(b_{k}^{(m)},B_{k}^{(m)}\right)C_{k,L_{m}}^{(m)}-p\!\left(b_{k}^{(m)},B_{k}^{(m)}\right), (7)

where bk(m)=b⁡(αk(m),Zk(m))b_{k}^{(m)}=b(\alpha_{k}^{(m)};Z_{k}^{(m)}), αi(m)=α\alpha_{i}^{(m)}=\alpha, and αk(m)=αcont\alpha_{k}^{(m)}=\alpha_{\mathrm{cont}} for k>ik>i. The allocation and payment rules 𝒲\mathcal{W} and pp are those defined in Section 3, with zero payment after a loss. For a lost auction, we set Ck,Lm(m)=0C_{k,L_{m}}^{(m)}=0.

The planning horizon limits the auctions for which decisions are simulated, not the delays of their conversions. A display won within the window may therefore contribute conversions after θi+H\theta_{i}+H, provided they occur before LmL_{m}, consistently with the environment’s reward reporting. Contributions from displays won before auction ii are omitted from the score because they do not depend on the candidate. The effects of simulated wins on subsequent opportunities are captured through the evolution of the carry-over context.

For each candidate, we average these returns over the MM rollouts:

Q^i​(α)=1M​∑m=1M∑k∈𝒩H(m)gk(m)​(α).\widehat{Q}_{i}(\alpha)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}_{H}^{(m)}}g_{k}^{(m)}(\alpha). (8)

Selecting the bid. We select the multiplier with the highest estimated net reward, breaking ties in favor of the smallest multiplier:

αi⋆=min⁡arg⁡maxα∈𝒜0​Q^i​(α),bi=b⁡(αi⋆,Zi).\alpha_{i}^{\star}=\min\arg\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{0}}\widehat{Q}_{i}(\alpha),\qquad b_{i}=b(\alpha_{i}^{\star};Z_{i}). (9)

After submitting bib_{i}, the bidder receives the auction feedback and repeats the optimization at the next opportunity. Pseudocode and implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

6 Experiments

Algorithms.

To illustrate the use of DynamAuction as a benchmark for bidding with dynamic valuations, we evaluate eight bidding policies, ranging from simple baselines to model-free reinforcement learning as well as our MPC approach. The policies are the following:

  • •

    Constant: Bids a fixed amount b∗b^{*} selected by grid search.

  • •

    FiPla, introduced by Bompaire et al. (2024) that bids the true myopic-optimal value V0​(Z)V_{0}(Z).

  • •

    Greedy Myopic, that estimates the marginal return of winning the current auction by comparing Monte Carlo rollouts that force a win or a loss, followed by a zero-bid continuation policy. The estimated difference is then used to determine the bid.

  • •

    Shading uses the same estimator as Greedy Myopic but scales the resulting bid by a constant multiplier α∗\alpha^{*} optimized through grid search.

  • •

    MPC, introduced in Section 5.

  • •

    Deep RL: We consider three model-free algorithms implemented with Stable-Baselines3 Raffin et al. (2021): PPO Schulman et al. (2017), SAC Haarnoja et al. (2018), and TD3 Fujimoto et al. (2018).

All policies are evaluated on the same 1,000 test campaigns to ensure consistent comparisons. For each RL algorithm, we select hyperparameters using 200 validation campaigns and train three models with different random seeds. We report the average performance across these three runs. Further experimental details are provided in Appendix C.

Scenario.

We choose a scenario in which current bidding decisions have lasting effects on future rewards, making planning a central aspect of the task. This can be modelled by advertising fatigue: a user repeatedly exposed to the same advertisement over a short period may become less receptive to subsequent impressions, with an effect that persists throughout the campaign. The bidder must therefore balance the expected reward of winning the current auction against its effect on the value of subsequent opportunities, making the timing and spacing of wins relevant to campaign performance. This is a deliberate modeling choice for our benchmark. Users of DynamAuction are free to specify alternative carry-over dynamics, reward kernels, and scenario parameters to study different mechanisms or applications.

Formally, all main experiments use the survival-second-price-exponential scenario, a second-price (Vickrey) auction environment with a random campaign duration T∼Exp⁡(1/η)T\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1/\eta), where η\eta is the mean duration. We consider η=50\eta=50, the corresponding test campaigns contain 47.7 auctions on average. Auction opportunities arrive according to a Poisson process of rate 1, and the competing bid is B∼LogNormal⁡(−1,1)B\sim\mathrm{LogNormal}(-1,1). A user feature vector u∼𝒩⁡(0,I3)u\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{3}) is drawn once per campaign, and a display feature vector x∼𝒩⁡(0,I3)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{3}) is drawn at each auction. Performance is reported as the mean episodic return over 1 000 test campaigns. The remaining parameters are listed in Tables 5 and 6.

Carry-over context and observations. To instantiate the commutative-monoid framework introduced in Section 3.2, we take the carry-over context to be the list of past wins:

Su(t−)={ti<t}.S_{u}(t^{-})=\{t_{i}<t\}. (10)

At time tt, the buyer only receives a scalar fatigue factor ϕ⁡(Su​(t−),t)\phi(S_{u}(t^{-}),t) computed from this history. The buyer therefore does not have access to the full carry-over context, making the scenario partially observable. For N≥1N\geq 1 past wins at times t1<⋯<tN<tt_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}<t, define

ϕ⁡(Su​(t−),t)=[∏i=2N(1−c​e−β⁡(ti−ti−1))]​(1−c​e−β⁡(t−tN)),c=0.9,β=1.\phi(S_{u}(t^{-}),t)=\left[\prod_{i=2}^{N}\left(1-ce^{-\beta(t_{i}-t_{i-1})}\right)\right]\left(1-ce^{-\beta(t-t_{N})}\right),\qquad c=0.9,\quad\beta=1. (11)

We use the empty-product convention and set ϕ⁡(∅,t)=1\phi(\varnothing,t)=1 before the first win. Each completed interval between consecutive wins contributes a fixed multiplicative penalty. Closely spaced wins cause a persistent reduction in subsequent conversion propensity within the campaign. If the current auction at time tt is won, its timestamp is added to the history after evaluating the current display’s reward kernel, so it affects later displays through their carry-over context. The observation fields are described in Table 4.

Delayed reward. There is no exogenous signal (yu≡0y_{u}\equiv 0) and no instantaneous reward component (κ=0\kappa=0). For delay τ>0\tau>0, the reward kernel is

𝒦⁡(u,x,S,0,t)​(d​τ)=clip⁡(ϕ⁡(S,t)​(𝟏⊤​u)​(𝟏⊤​x),0,1)​e−τ​d​τ,\mathcal{K}(u,x,S,0,t)(\mathrm{d}\tau)=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\phi(S,t)(\mathbf{1}^{\top}u)(\mathbf{1}^{\top}x),0,1\right)\,e^{-\tau}\,\mathrm{d}\tau,

Conditional on the realized campaign end TT, the expected conversion reward attributable to a display won at ti<Tt_{i}<T is

Vioracle=clip⁡(ϕ⁡(S,t)​(𝟏⊤​u)​(𝟏⊤​x),0,1)​(1−e−(T−ti)).V_{i}^{\mathrm{oracle}}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\phi(S,t)(\mathbf{1}^{\top}u)(\mathbf{1}^{\top}x),0,1\right)\left(1-e^{-(T-t_{i})}\right).

We call this quantity the oracle value because it depends on the realized end time TT, which is unknown to the bidder. The oracle value is available to FiPla but hidden from the other agents (Table 3).

Results.

Table 1 and Figure 2 report the performance of the different policies. MPC outperforms the tuned Shading baseline when the planning horizon is sufficiently long (H≥25H\geq 25). The best configuration, MPC(H=35H=35, M=60M=60, αcont=0.4\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.4), achieves a mean episodic return of 4.334.33, compared with 3.683.68 for Shading and 2.822.82 for FiPla. The gain over Shading is +0.65±0.13+0.65\pm 0.13. With a shorter planning horizon (H=10H=10), the improvement is smaller but remains positive (+0.26±0.11+0.26\pm 0.11). Using a shaded continuation policy (αcont=0.4\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.4) also improves MPC performance, although the gains are smaller. The deep RL algorithms perform worse than Shading on average. Their performance is also sensitive to training: PPO shows substantial variability across seeds, one of the three TD3 runs converges to a policy that never bids, and SAC wins considerably more auctions than FiPla but achieves a lower return. Additional experiments are reported in Appendix D.

7 Conclusion

We introduced a generic model for describing dynamic value in repeated auctions, along with DynamAuction, an RL environment for studying sequential bidding. The environment is challenging for deep reinforcement learning methods while accommodating settings that can be studied analytically, as in Heymann et al. (2024). On our benchmark, which illustrates the motivation for planning in this setting, simple shading and model-predictive control policies outperform the tested deep RL methods. Our design focuses on isolating the effects of dynamic value. Accordingly, we use synthetic data and leave budget and ROI constraints outside the scope of this work.
