Appendix A Environment implementation and configuration

DynamAuction provides seven predefined scenarios (Table 2), each of which can be customized using the parameters listed in Tables 5 and 6. Our main experiments use the survival-second-price-exponential scenario. Additional experiments consider immediate conversions and the saturation and recency scenarios (Appendix D).

A.1 Gymnasium Interface and Wrappers

DynamAuction follows the Gymnasium API and can be used with Stable-Baselines3. For RL training, we apply three wrappers in order: remove the oracle expected reward from the observation, flatten the remaining observation fields into a vector, and clip bids to [0,bmax][0,b_{\max}] (Table 3).

A.2 Observation and Action Spaces

Table 4 describes the observation fields provided by the environment. The user features in ZiZ_{i} (Section 3.4) consist of an observed user vector uobs∈ℝdou_{\mathrm{obs}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}}, with do≤dd_{o}\leq d, while the reward kernel depends on the full vector u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. In all our experiments, the user features are fully observed (do=dd_{o}=d).

A.3 Episode initialization and reward reporting

At the start of each episode, the environment samples the campaign horizon TT and the auction times over [0,T][0,T]. Each step corresponds to an auction and advances the simulation to the next auction time. When an auction is won, the conversion times of the corresponding display are sampled. Delayed conversions are reported at the next auction, without identifying the display that generated them. Let CinowC_{i}^{\mathrm{now}} denote the number of immediate conversions from winning auction ii, and C[i−1,i]delayedC^{\mathrm{delayed}}_{[i-1,i]} the number of delayed conversions occurring in (θi−1,θi](\theta_{i-1},\theta_{i}], with θ0=0\theta_{0}=0. The reward reported at step ii is

r~i=v​Wi​Cinow−pi+v​C[i−1,i]delayed,\tilde{r}_{i}=vW_{i}C_{i}^{\mathrm{now}}-p_{i}+vC^{\mathrm{delayed}}_{[i-1,i]}, (12)

where vv is the value of a conversion, WiW_{i} indicates whether auction ii is won, and pi=p⁡(bi,Bi)p_{i}=p(b_{i},B_{i}) is the payment, which is zero if the auction is lost. Unlike the expected reward rj​(h)r_{j}(h) associated with a single display in Equation (3), the step reward r~i\tilde{r}_{i} may include conversions from several earlier wins. The episode ends after the last auction before TT, and conversions occurring after this auction are not credited, even if they occur before TT.

Appendix B Bidding Algorithms

We provide pseudocode and implementation details for MPC, followed by the GreedyMyopic and Shading baselines.

B.1 MPC

At auction ii, which takes place at time θi\theta_{i}, the bidder receives the observation ZiZ_{i}. The learned estimator V^0​(Zi)\widehat{V}_{0}(Z_{i}) predicts the conversion value of the current display, before payment. MPC uses this estimate to construct candidate bids, then compares them by simulating their consequences.

Candidate bids and future decisions.

Let 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} be a finite set of nonnegative multipliers. For each α∈𝒜0\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{0}, the candidate bid is max⁡(0,α​V^0​(Zi))\max(0,\alpha\widehat{V}_{0}(Z_{i})). We evaluate this bid with MM simulated trajectories, called rollouts. Each rollout processes the current auction and the following auctions up to time θi+H\theta_{i}+H, where the planning horizon HH is measured in time units.

After the current auction, bids follow a fixed continuation policy. At a later simulated auction kk, this policy bids max⁡(0,αcont​V^0​(Zk))\max(0,\alpha_{\rm cont}\widehat{V}_{0}(Z_{k})), where ZkZ_{k} is the observation reached in that rollout and αcont\alpha_{\rm cont} is a fixed nonnegative multiplier. Thus, only the first multiplier α\alpha is optimized; subsequent bids depend on the simulated observations through V^0\widehat{V}_{0}.

Simulated campaigns and shared random draws.

Each rollout starts from a copy of the current simulator state, including past wins and pending conversions. The current observation is kept fixed, while future events are sampled anew. For the exponential campaign durations used here, rollout mm draws a remaining duration Tm′∼Exp⁡(1/η)T^{\prime}_{m}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1/\eta), where η\eta is the mean campaign length. It then samples the future auction times and exogenous events up to θi+Tm′\theta_{i}+T^{\prime}_{m}. We write θk(m)\theta_{k}^{(m)} for the auction times in this sampled campaign, with θi(m)=θi\theta_{i}^{(m)}=\theta_{i}.

The same sampled campaign is used for every candidate α\alpha. Competing bids and future display features are drawn from separate random streams, and conversion draws are indexed by auction. This keeps the random inputs at auction kk aligned across candidates, even when earlier auction outcomes differ. The conversion outcomes can still differ, because their probabilities depend on the history of wins. These common random numbers are used to reduce the variance of differences between candidate returns.

Scoring a rollout.

For each candidate α\alpha, rollout mm simulates the current auction and subsequent auctions up to the planning horizon HH. Its return is the net reward of the displays won during this window:

R(m)​(α)=∑k=ikend(m)𝒲⁡(bk(m),Bk(m))​(Ck(m)−p⁡(bk(m),Bk(m))),bk(m)=αk(m)​V^0​(Zk(m)),R^{(m)}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=i}^{k_{\mathrm{end}}^{(m)}}\mathcal{W}\bigl(b_{k}^{(m)},B_{k}^{(m)}\bigr)\Bigl(C_{k}^{(m)}-p\bigl(b_{k}^{(m)},B_{k}^{(m)}\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad b_{k}^{(m)}=\alpha_{k}^{(m)}\,\widehat{V}_{0}\bigl(Z_{k}^{(m)}\bigr),

where αi(m)=α\alpha_{i}^{(m)}=\alpha and αk(m)=αcont\alpha_{k}^{(m)}=\alpha_{\rm cont} for k>ik>i. Here, kend(m)k_{\mathrm{end}}^{(m)} is the last auction within the planning horizon, and Ck(m)C_{k}^{(m)} is the value of the conversions generated by the display won at auction kk that occur before the last auction of the simulated campaign, at time t(Nm)t^{(N_{m})}.

Importantly, the planning horizon limits which auctions are simulated, not which conversions are counted. A display won within the planning horizon may generate conversions after HH, and these are included in its return as long as they occur before t(Nm)t^{(N_{m})}, consistently with the environment’s reward reporting. Conversions from displays won before auction ii are omitted because they do not depend on the candidate α\alpha.

The estimated return of each candidate is then

Q^​(α)=1M​∑m=1MR(m)​(α).\widehat{Q}(\alpha)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}R^{(m)}(\alpha).

MPC selects the candidate with the largest mean score, breaking ties in favor of the smallest multiplier. It submits this bid and repeats the procedure at the next real auction. Algorithm 1 gives the steps.

Special cases.

With 𝒜0={1}\mathcal{A}_{0}=\{1\}, MPC returns the bid max⁡(0,V^0​(Zi))\max(0,\widehat{V}_{0}(Z_{i})); using the oracle V0V_{0} gives the FiPla bid. With H=0H=0, each rollout evaluates only the current auction, including its delayed conversions credited before LmL_{m}. In a second-price auction, α=1\alpha=1 is optimal in expectation if the valuation is exact for these credited conversions and 1∈𝒜01\in\mathcal{A}_{0}. A learned valuation and a finite number of rollouts can lead to a different choice.

Computational cost.

Each decision evaluates |𝒜0|​M|\mathcal{A}_{0}|M rollouts. The number of auctions processed in each rollout depends on HH, the arrival process and the sampled campaign duration. The rollouts use the simulator’s dynamics directly; V^0\widehat{V}_{0} is the learned component used to set bids.

B.2 GreedyMyopic

GreedyMyopic estimates the conversion value of winning the current auction, assuming that no further auctions will be won. Let π0\pi_{0} denote the continuation policy that bids zero at every subsequent auction.

At auction ii, we run MM pairs of simulations from the current simulator state. In each pair, one simulation forces a win at auction ii and the other forces a loss. Both then follow π0\pi_{0} until the last auction of the simulated campaign. They share the same remaining duration Tm′∼Exp⁡(1/η)T^{\prime}_{m}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1/\eta), future auction times and exogenous events, and start with the same noise seed ωm\omega_{m}.

Let Rwin(m)R_{\mathrm{win}}^{(m)} and Rloss(m)R_{\mathrm{loss}}^{(m)} denote the total conversion value credited in these two simulations. Payments are excluded, since the quantity being estimated is the display’s value before payment. As in the environment, conversions occurring after the last auction are not credited. The bid is

bi=Δ^=max⁡(0,1M​∑m=1M(Rwin(m)−Rloss(m))).b_{i}=\hat{\Delta}=\max\!\left(0,\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(R_{\mathrm{win}}^{(m)}-R_{\mathrm{loss}}^{(m)}\right)\right).

The paired simulations use common random numbers to cancel the contributions of previously won displays, as detailed in Remark 1.

Remark 1 (Common Random Numbers).

The scenario seed fixes the remaining campaign duration, auction times and exogenous events. The noise seed ωm\omega_{m} initializes the single generator used for competing bids, display features and conversions. The forced-win simulation draws conversions for the current display, which shifts the subsequent draws of this generator. These later draws do not affect conversion rewards because π0\pi_{0} wins no further auctions. Conversions already pending at auction ii are copied unchanged into both simulations and are credited at the same auction times. Their contributions therefore cancel in Rwin(m)−Rloss(m)R_{\mathrm{win}}^{(m)}-R_{\mathrm{loss}}^{(m)}, leaving the conversion value credited to the current display. This value remains random, and Δ^\hat{\Delta} averages it over the MM pairs.

B.3 Shading

Shading uses the same value estimate Δ^\hat{\Delta} as GreedyMyopic (Algorithm 2), but multiplies it by a fixed factor α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1]. This reduces the bid to account for the effect of winning the current auction on the value of future opportunities. When α=1\alpha=1, Shading is equivalent to GreedyMyopic.

Appendix C Experimental details

C.1 Scenario configuration

Tables 5 and 6 list the configurable components of DynamAuction and their preset values. The main experiments use this preset with η=50\eta=50.

C.2 Evaluation protocol

All policies are evaluated on the same 1 000 test campaigns, generated with environment seeds 0–999. This allows us to compare policies on identical campaigns, rather than on independently sampled ones. For stochastic policies, campaign ss uses the policy seed s+1000s+1000.

Training and model selection use different campaigns. The MPC valuation head is trained on 1 000 FiPla campaigns (seeds 10 000–10 999), while the RL agents generate their training campaigns from their own random streams. Intermediate evaluations during RL training use seeds ≥10 000\geq 10\,000. RL hyperparameters and checkpoints are selected using 200 validation campaigns (seeds 20 000–20 199). Each selected RL configuration is then trained with three different random seeds.

We report mean rewards with 95% confidence intervals, written as the mean ±1.96σ^/n\pm 1.96\,\hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{n}, where σ^\hat{\sigma} is the sample standard deviation over the nn test campaigns. For comparisons between policies AA and BB, we compute the reward difference RA​(s)−RB​(s)R_{A}(s)-R_{B}(s) on each campaign ss and use the standard deviation of these paired differences to construct the confidence interval. For RL policies, R⁡(s)R(s) is the average reward of the three trained models on campaign ss. Since both policies face the same campaigns, pairing reduces the variability due to differences in campaign length and user characteristics, yielding narrower confidence intervals for their performance differences.

C.3 Hyperparameters and training

We report the configurations used in the experiments and how their parameters were selected.

MPC.

MPC evaluates candidate bids using the multiplier grid 𝒜0={0.1,0.2,…,1.0}\mathcal{A}_{0}=\{0.1,0.2,\dots,1.0\}, with ties resolved in favor of the smallest multiplier. We consider planning horizons H∈{10,25,35}H\in\{10,25,35\}, M∈{60,80}M\in\{60,80\} rollouts per candidate, and continuation multipliers αcont∈{1,0.4}\alpha_{\rm cont}\in\{1,0.4\}, where 0.40.4 is the multiplier selected for Shading. Unless otherwise specified, αcont=1\alpha_{\rm cont}=1 in all tables and figures.

As described in Algorithm 1, candidate bids are compared using common random numbers for competing bids, display features, and conversions. Each rollout is scored by the net reward of the displays won within the planning horizon, including their conversions occurring before the last auction of the simulated campaign.

MPC uses a learned valuation head V^0\widehat{V}_{0} to estimate the oracle value V0V_{0} from observations that exclude V0V_{0} itself. We train this estimator on 1 000 FiPla campaigns, corresponding to 49 358 auctions at η=50\eta=50, with 15% of the data held out for validation. Training uses Adam with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, a batch size of 256, and 500 epochs.

We compare MLPs with two hidden layers of 32, 64, or 128 units, using ReLU or Leaky ReLU activations (Figure 3 and Table 7). Although the larger networks achieve lower training MSE (0.00097 and 0.00068, compared with 0.00147 for 32-32 ReLU), their test errors are higher (0.00208 and 0.00209, compared with 0.00184). Leaky ReLU performs similarly to ReLU (test MSE 0.00181 for 32-32 Leaky ReLU). We therefore use the 32-32 ReLU network, which has the lowest test error among the ReLU architectures and requires only 1 505 parameters, compared with 5 057 and 18 305 for the larger networks. Its smaller size also reduces the cost of the repeated predictions made during MPC rollouts.

GreedyMyopic and Shading.

Both policies estimate the value of the current display as the mean difference between MM Monte Carlo rollouts that force a win and MM that force a loss, continued with the bid 0; each pair of rollouts shares its random numbers, so that environment noise cancels in the difference. The shading multiplier is selected by a grid search over α∈{0.1,0.2,…,1.0}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,\dots,1.0\} with M=20M=20 rollouts, on the 1 000 test campaigns: the best value is α∗=0.4\alpha^{*}=0.4 (Figure 4), and GreedyMyopic is Shading with α=1\alpha=1 and M=20M=20. Unlike the RL hyperparameters, which are selected on validation campaigns, the Shading multiplier (and hence αcont=0.4\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.4 in MPC) and the constant bid are selected on the test campaigns, which slightly favors these policies.

Constant bidder.

The constant bid is selected by a two-stage grid search on the 1 000 test campaigns, first on a coarse grid of step 0.10.1 over [0,1.5][0,1.5], then on a grid of step 0.010.01 within ±0.1\pm 0.1 of the best coarse value: b∗=0.11b^{*}=0.11 (Figure 5).

C.4 Deep RL training details

Observations and actions.

PPO, SAC, and TD3 receive flattened observations from which the oracle value used by FiPla has been removed. This value is unavailable during both training and evaluation. Observations and rewards are normalized using VecNormalize, and bids are clipped to [0,5][0,5]. We use the default Stable-Baselines3 network architectures: two hidden layers of 64 units with tanh\tanh activations for PPO, and two hidden layers of 256 units with ReLU activations for SAC and TD3.

Hyperparameter search.

We select the hyperparameters of each algorithm through a grid search at η=50\eta=50, using the Inria Margaret cluster. The search covers 144 configurations for PPO, 48 for SAC, and 96 for TD3. The tested values and fixed parameters are listed in Table 8.

Each configuration is trained for 5×1065\times 10^{6} timesteps with seed 42 and four parallel environments. During training, we evaluate the policy on 20 campaigns every 10410^{4} timesteps and save the checkpoint with the highest evaluation reward. At the end of training, we compare this checkpoint with the final checkpoint on a separate set of 200 validation campaigns, using the normalization statistics saved with each checkpoint. For each algorithm, we select the configuration and checkpoint with the highest mean validation reward.

Final training.

Once the hyperparameters have been selected, we train the chosen configuration again for 10710^{7} timesteps with three different seeds (42, 43, and 44). For each training, we compare the best intermediate checkpoint and the final checkpoint on the 200 validation campaigns, then evaluate the better one on the 1 000 test campaigns. The results reported for each RL algorithm are averaged over these three independently trained models.

Table 8 reports the selected hyperparameters, their validation rewards during the search, and the test reward obtained by each of the three final trainings.

Results of the hyperparameter search.

Figure 6 shows the validation reward obtained for each tested configuration. Most TD3 configurations converge to policies that never bid (82 out of 96), as do 5 of the 48 SAC configurations. PPO is less affected by this failure mode, although its final performance still depends on the training seed, as discussed below.

Training behavior.

Figure 7 shows the learning curves of the three final trainings for each algorithm. The runs reveal substantial differences across algorithms and training seeds.

TD3 is particularly unstable: one of its three final trainings converges to a policy that never bids, as observed in most configurations during the search. Once its deterministic bid falls to zero, the agent stops winning auctions and does not recover in these runs.

PPO also shows substantial variability across seeds, with test rewards of 3.523.52, 3.533.53, and 1.841.84 despite using the same hyperparameters. SAC, by contrast, reaches its final performance level within approximately 10610^{6} steps, but learns a policy that wins many cheap auctions and keeps users fatigued.

Longer PPO training.

To check whether PPO benefits from a larger training budget, we extend the selected configuration to 5×1075\times 10^{7} timesteps, using the same three training seeds. Figure 8 shows that test performance decreases over the extended runs. For example, seed 42 achieves a test reward of 3.593.59 after 5×1065\times 10^{6} steps, 3.313.31 after 10710^{7} steps, and 2.612.61 after 5×1075\times 10^{7} steps. Increasing the training budget therefore does not improve PPO’s performance in this experiment.

Appendix D Additional experiments

D.1 Bidding under varying auction frequency and recovering user fatigue

We consider a variant of the main scenario to test whether MPC adjusts its bids when the cost of winning changes over the course of a campaign. Two components are modified :

  • •

    Recovering fatigue. Each past win at time tit_{i} reduces the value of future displays through a factor that gradually returns to 1:

    Su(t−)=∏i:ti<t(1−ce−β⁡(t−ti)),c=0.9,β=0.3.S_{u}(t^{-})=\prod_{i:\,t_{i}<t}\bigl(1-ce^{-\beta(t-t_{i})}\bigr),\qquad c=0.9,\quad\beta=0.3.

    This corresponds to Equation (1) with the monoid ([0,1],×,1)([0,1],\times,1) and decay map γ⁡(xi,ti,t)=1−c​e−β⁡(t−ti)\gamma(x_{i},t_{i},t)=1-ce^{-\beta(t-t_{i})}. Each factor starts at 0.10.1 immediately after a win and approaches 1 independently of subsequent wins. After five time units, a win still reduces conversion propensity by about 20%. The reward kernel uses Su​(t−)S_{u}(t^{-}) instead of ϕ\phi, giving a conversion propensity clip⁡(Su​(t−)​(𝟏⊤​u)​(𝟏⊤​x),0,1)\mathrm{clip}\bigl(S_{u}(t^{-})(\mathbf{1}^{\top}u)(\mathbf{1}^{\top}x),0,1\bigr). The bidder observes Su​(t−)S_{u}(t^{-}), but not the past win times that determine its future evolution.

  • •

    Higher auction frequency at the start of the campaign. Auctions arrive according to a non-homogeneous Poisson process with rate 10 on [0,10)[0,10) and rate 1 thereafter, instead of rate 1 throughout the campaign. The campaign duration remains exponential with mean η=50\eta=50. This produces 131 auctions per campaign on average, including 92 during the initial high-frequency period.

During the first ten time units, auctions arrive roughly 0.1 time units apart, so fatigue from successive wins accumulates before it can dissipate. Later, auctions are less frequent and users have more time to recover. Winning an auction can therefore reduce the value of many more future opportunities early in the campaign than later on, making a fixed shading multiplier potentially suboptimal.

Experimental protocol.

All policies are evaluated on the same 200 test campaigns (environment seeds 0–199, policy seed s+1000s+1000 for campaign ss). Comparisons are paired, as in the main benchmark, but use one fifth as many campaigns, giving confidence intervals approximately 2.2 times wider.

Shading uses M=20M=20 rollouts, with its multiplier selected from {0.1,…,1}\{0.1,\ldots,1\} on these test campaigns (α=0.6\alpha=0.6). GreedyMyopic corresponds to α=1\alpha=1, while the two-stage search for the constant bidder gives b=0.09b=0.09.

MPC uses M=60M=60 rollouts per candidate, with α∈{0.1,…,1}\alpha\in\{0.1,\ldots,1\}, and a 32-32 ReLU valuation head trained on 1 000 FiPla campaigns of this scenario, following the main benchmark procedure. We compare three continuation policies:

  • •

    Fixed: αcont=0.6\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.6, the selected Shading multiplier, with H∈{5,15,25}H\in\{5,15,25\}.

  • •

    Shared: the candidate multiplier α\alpha is also used for subsequent bids in each rollout, with H∈{5,10,15,25}H\in\{5,10,15,25\}.

  • •

    Two-phase: αcont=0.3\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.3 before t=10t=10 and 0.70.7 thereafter, with H∈{5,15,25}H\in\{5,15,25\}.

The two-phase coefficients are selected by searching pairs (a1,a2)(a_{1},a_{2}) on a grid with step 0.10.1, using an oracle policy that bids a1​V0a_{1}V_{0} before t=10t=10 and a2​V0a_{2}V_{0} afterwards. Selection uses 200 validation campaigns (seeds 20 000–20 199).

For PPO, we conduct a smaller hyperparameter search centered on the configuration selected in the main benchmark. The initial grid combines learning rates {5×10−5,10−4,3×10−4}\{5\times 10^{-5},10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4}\}, rollout lengths {256,512}\{256,512\} and optimization epochs {5,10}\{5,10\} (12 configurations). Since its best configuration uses 512 steps and 10 epochs, at the edge of this grid, we extend the search to learning rates {10−4,2×10−4,3×10−4}\{10^{-4},2\times 10^{-4},3\times 10^{-4}\}, rollout lengths {512,1024,2048}\{512,1024,2048\} and epochs {5,10,20}\{5,10,20\}. This adds 23 new configurations, for 35 in total. The entropy coefficient remains 0 and γ=0.99\gamma=0.99; all other settings follow Table 8.

Each configuration is trained for 3×1063\times 10^{6} steps and evaluated on 200 validation campaigns using its best intermediate and final checkpoints. The selected configuration (learning rate 10−410^{-4}, 1 024 steps per update, 5 epochs, final checkpoint) is retrained with three seeds for 5×1065\times 10^{6} steps, and each training is evaluated on the 200 test campaigns. Both training budgets are shorter than in the main benchmark (5×1065\times 10^{6} and 10710^{7} steps, respectively). SAC and TD3 are not evaluated here, as both performed below PPO in the main benchmark.

Results.

Shading improves on FiPla by +0.70±0.28+0.70\pm 0.28 (+13%). MPC performs better than Shading across the three continuation policies. Its best variant (H=5H=5, M=60M=60, αcont=0.6\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.6) gains +0.44±0.26+0.44\pm 0.26 (+7%) over Shading and +1.14±0.26+1.14\pm 0.26 (+21%) over FiPla. The 95% confidence interval for the gain over Shading excludes zero for 8 of the 10 MPC variants.

MPC bids more selectively during the high-frequency period, winning 5.7% of auctions, compared with 6.6% for Shading and 7.7% for FiPla. After t=10t=10, its win rate rises to 17.9%, close to Shading’s 17.6%. With the shared continuation, MPC selects an average multiplier of 0.45 before t=10t=10 and 0.74 afterwards, close to the oracle two-phase coefficients (0.3,0.7)(0.3,0.7).

However, allowing the continuation policy to vary with time brings no clear improvement over the fixed multiplier αcont=0.6\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.6. Most variants perform similarly, and the shared continuation at H=25H=25 is the only one significantly below the best fixed-continuation variant (−0.37±0.23-0.37\pm 0.23). Replanning at every auction appears sufficient to adapt the current bid to the campaign phase, without requiring a time-dependent continuation policy or a longer planning horizon.

PPO remains below Shading on average (−1.14±0.39-1.14\pm 0.39) and below the best MPC (−1.58±0.41-1.58\pm 0.41). Two of its three trainings outperform FiPla (+0.41±0.33+0.41\pm 0.33 and +0.33±0.38+0.33\pm 0.38) but remain below Shading (−0.29±0.29-0.29\pm 0.29 and −0.37±0.36-0.37\pm 0.36). The third learns to bid too little, winning only 5.2% of auctions, compared with 9.3–12.2% for the other policies except Constant.

The selected PPO run reaches a validation reward of 6.62 after 3×1063\times 10^{6} steps, but its three retrainings achieve only 6.10, 2.46 and 6.29 on the same validation campaigns after 5×1065\times 10^{6} steps. The high reward of the selected run thus appears optimistic, reflecting the selection of the best among 35 configurations on only 200 validation campaigns.

D.2 Computational cost and performance of bidding policies

Table 10 reports the time to compute one bid, measured on the same 80 decision states of the main scenario (η=50\eta=50), on one CPU core of a laptop (Intel Core Ultra 7 265H) and of a cluster node (Intel Xeon E5-2695 v3); the time per campaign is the time per bid times 47.7 auctions. MPC’s cost is linear in the number of rollouts MM and in the horizon HH (each rollout simulates the next HH time units), whereas its reward saturates around H=25H=25 and M=40M=40–8080; the best setting, MPC(H=35H=35, M=60M=60, αcont=0.4\alpha_{\rm cont}=0.4), costs about 2.3 s per bid on the laptop. Changing αcont\alpha_{\rm cont} does not change the cost. One prediction of the valuation head takes 0.130.13 ms, and the RL policies need less than 1 ms per bid.

D.3 Robustness of MPC to valuation errors and fewer rollouts

We study how errors in the learned valuation head V^0\widehat{V}_{0} and the number of planning rollouts affect MPC’s performance. Our reference is MPC(H=25H=25, M=80M=80, αcont=1\alpha_{\rm cont}=1), using the 32-32 ReLU head trained on 1 000 FiPla campaigns. We consider four types of changes (Table 11): (i) multiplicative noise, scaling each prediction by eσ​ε−σ2/2e^{\sigma\varepsilon-\sigma^{2}/2}, with ε∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and σ∈{0.1,0.25,0.5,1}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\}; (ii) heads trained on only 10, 30, 100, or 300 campaigns; (iii) misspecified heads that ignore fatigue (S=1S=1), are trained with higher competition (LogNormal⁡(0,1)\mathrm{LogNormal}(0,1)), or have their predictions multiplied by 0.5 or 2; and (iv) fewer planning rollouts, keeping the reference head unchanged.

All variants are evaluated on the same 1 000 test campaigns, with paired differences and 95% confidence intervals. The valuation-head experiments also use the same rollout random numbers as the reference. Prediction errors are measured against the oracle V0V_{0} on auctions with V0>0.05V_{0}>0.05.

MPC tolerates moderate valuation errors (Table 11, Figure 9). Heads trained on 100 or 300 campaigns perform close to the reference (−0.09±0.09-0.09\pm 0.09 and −0.03±0.09-0.03\pm 0.09). Multiplicative noise reduces the reward by about 0.17 for σ≤0.25\sigma\leq 0.25 and 0.35 for σ=0.5\sigma=0.5, but MPC still outperforms Shading. With σ=1\sigma=1, it falls to Shading’s level; with only 10 training campaigns, it performs substantially worse. Ignoring fatigue reduces the reward by 0.48±0.110.48\pm 0.11, bringing MPC close to Shading, whereas a head trained under higher competition performs similarly to the reference (−0.05±0.08-0.05\pm 0.08).

Errors in the scale of V^0\widehat{V}_{0} have asymmetric effects. Halving its predictions does not reduce performance (+0.07±0.10+0.07\pm 0.10), as it gives a finer grid of candidate bids in the relevant range. Doubling them leads to excessive bids, including during rollout continuation, and reduces the reward by 0.45±0.120.45\pm 0.12. Reducing the number of rollouts has a smaller effect than large valuation errors: using M=20M=20–6060 instead of 80 lowers the reward by 0.13–0.24, while even M=10M=10 remains above Shading (+0.20±0.11+0.20\pm 0.11).

D.4 Evaluating bidding policies without delayed rewards

We evaluate a variant of the main scenario in which conversions occur immediately after a winning auction, with the same probability ff as in the original scenario (Table 12). This removes delayed credit assignment while keeping the fatigue dynamics, competition, and campaign lengths unchanged. The variant, survival-second-price-exponential-immediate, also ensures that no conversion is lost after the last auction. MPC uses a valuation head trained on this scenario, while the RL agents follow the same hyperparameter search and training protocol as in the main benchmark.

With immediate conversions, PPO outperforms all myopic baselines, including Shading (+0.25±0.10+0.25\pm 0.10), but remains below MPC (−0.34±0.10-0.34\pm 0.10). Thus, removing delayed feedback does not eliminate the advantage of MPC, which can still plan around the effects of fatigue on future auctions. TD3 remains unstable: one training reaches 3.93, above Shading, while the other two converge to policies that never bid, as did 44 of its 96 hyperparameter configurations during the search.

Immediate conversions also prevent rewards from being lost after the last auction, unlike in the main scenario. Since the two scenarios do not share the same random draws, performance comparisons are made within each scenario.

D.5 Evaluating bidding policies against the optimal policy under saturation and recency

We consider two simpler scenarios in which the optimal bidding policy can be computed by dynamic programming (DP). Neither scenario has user or display features, and the carry-over state is one-dimensional. They differ in how past wins affect conversion probability:

  • •

    Saturation: p(n)=e−n/10p(n)=e^{-n/10}, where nn is the number of past wins.

  • •

    Recency: p⁡(τ)=1−e−0.5​τp(\tau)=1-e^{-0.5\tau}, where τ\tau is the time since the last win.

Both scenarios use exponentially distributed conversion delays with rate 0.50.5 and competing bids drawn from LogNormal⁡(−1,1)\mathrm{LogNormal}(-1,1).

We compare the bidding policies with the DP optimum on the same 1 000 test campaigns. Unless otherwise stated, MPC uses M=60M=60 rollouts and αcont=1\alpha_{\rm cont}=1, while the RL agents follow the training protocol of the main benchmark. We also evaluate PPO with the time since the last win added to its observations, and a diagnostic Cooldown policy that bids the oracle V0V_{0} except during a fixed period after each win. The tables report the fraction of the improvement over FiPla achieved by each policy, defined as (R−RFiPla)/(RDP−RFiPla)(R-R_{\mathrm{FiPla}})/(R_{\mathrm{DP}}-R_{\mathrm{FiPla}}), where RR denotes the mean episode reward.

Computing the optimal policy.

In both scenarios, the campaign duration is exponential with mean η=50\eta=50, giving a termination rate h=1/η=0.02h=1/\eta=0.02. Auction arrivals have rate 1. Because the remaining campaign duration is memoryless, the optimal policy depends only on the current state ss: the number of past wins nn for saturation, or the time since the last win τ\tau for recency. Before the first win, τ=∞\tau=\infty and p⁡(τ)=1p(\tau)=1.

A display won in state ss has expected conversion value

r⁡(s)=p⁡(s)​δδ+h,r(s)=p(s)\frac{\delta}{\delta+h},

where δ=0.5\delta=0.5 is the conversion-delay rate. The factor δ/(δ+h)\delta/(\delta+h) accounts for the probability that the conversion occurs before the campaign ends.

The probability of reaching another auction before the campaign ends is q=1/(1+h)q=1/(1+h). Conditional on reaching it, the elapsed time is G∼Exp⁡(1+h)G\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1+h). A win changes the state to swin′=n+1s^{\prime}_{\rm win}=n+1 in saturation or swin′=Gs^{\prime}_{\rm win}=G in recency; after a loss, the state is slose′=ns^{\prime}_{\rm lose}=n or slose′=τ+Gs^{\prime}_{\rm lose}=\tau+G, respectively.

In a second-price auction, the optimal bid is the marginal value of winning:

b∗​(s)=max⁡(D⁡(s),0),D⁡(s)=r⁡(s)+q⁡(𝔼​V​(swin′)−𝔼​V​(slose′)),b^{*}(s)=\max(D(s),0),\qquad D(s)=r(s)+q\bigl(\mathbb{E}V(s^{\prime}_{\rm win})-\mathbb{E}V(s^{\prime}_{\rm lose})\bigr),

where V⁡(s)V(s) is the optimal expected future reward and satisfies

V⁡(s)=q​𝔼​V​(slose′)+𝔼⁡[(D⁡(s)−B)+],B∼LogNormal⁡(−1,1).V(s)=q\,\mathbb{E}V(s^{\prime}_{\rm lose})+\mathbb{E}\bigl[(D(s)-B)^{+}\bigr],\qquad B\sim\mathrm{LogNormal}(-1,1).

The last expectation has a closed form. For saturation, we solve the Bellman equation by backward induction from n=200n=200, where conversion probability is negligible, using bisection to solve for each V⁡(n)V(n). For recency, we use value iteration on a grid τ∈[0,60]\tau\in[0,60] with step 0.020.02, stopping when the maximum change falls below 10−910^{-9}.

The resulting policy bids b∗​(s)b^{*}(s) at every auction. Since it uses the known model, it provides an optimal reference in expectation, subject to numerical approximation and test-sample variability. Table 16 reports its effective shading multiplier α∗​(s)=b∗​(s)/r⁡(s)\alpha^{*}(s)=b^{*}(s)/r(s).

Why constant shading is close to optimal.

In both scenarios, the optimal bid is approximately a fixed fraction of the myopic value r⁡(s)r(s) (Table 16). The effective multiplier α∗​(s)=b∗​(s)/r⁡(s)\alpha^{*}(s)=b^{*}(s)/r(s) ranges from 0.39 to 0.66 for the first 15 wins in saturation, and from 0.53 to 0.64 for the recency states considered. A single shading multiplier therefore approximates the optimal policy well. Indeed, Shading is statistically indistinguishable from the DP optimum in both scenarios: +0.03±0.08+0.03\pm 0.08 in saturation and −0.09±0.12-0.09\pm 0.12 in recency.

With M=60M=60 rollouts, MPC remains below Shading in both scenarios. Increasing MM to 1 000 substantially reduces this gap, particularly in recency, where MPC matches Shading (+0.00±0.12+0.00\pm 0.12). This suggests that the accuracy of MPC’s rollout estimates matters when the optimal multiplier varies little across states.

Effect of state representation on PPO.

PPO performs close to Shading in saturation, where the number of past wins is directly available in its observation. In recency, however, PPO receives the current time and the time of the last win as separate inputs (with −1000-1000 indicating no previous win). Its bids barely depend on their difference, the time elapsed since the last win, and its performance is close to that of a constant bidder. Adding this elapsed time explicitly to the observation, while keeping the same hyperparameters and training seeds, improves PPO’s reward by about 0.6 and brings it close to Shading (−0.14±0.10-0.14\pm 0.10). The gap in this scenario is therefore largely explained by the state representation.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: it does

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: it does

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: it does

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: it does

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: it does

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: it does

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: it does

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: it does

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: we reviewed it

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: help practitioners and theoreticians to better train RL model on repeated auctions with dynamic value.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
